tips.title: It is never a set work, and never wider listening
tips.body: The specification is explicit: the unfamiliar piece is neither a set work nor one of the suggested wider listening pieces. It is chosen because it is **stylistically close to a set work**, so the work you have already done is exactly what you use. Ask yourself which set work it resembles, and answer from there.

tips.title: A skeleton score is a summary, not the music
tips.body: Appendix 3 defines it as a notational summary that **usually shows one leading part rather than the whole texture**. So the absence of a second line on the page is not evidence that nothing else is playing. Use the score for bar numbers, key, metre and chord symbols; use your ears for everything else.

tips.title: Answer in the number of words asked for
tips.body: These are one-word, short-response and grid questions, not an essay. "Identify the texture" wants one word. "Any two of the following" wants two bullet points. Sentences of explanation earn nothing extra here and cost you the time you need for the twelve-mark question at the end.

tips.title: Check the bar numbers before you answer
tips.body: Every part names a place: bars 1 to 4, bar 5 beat 2, bars 23 to 27. Marks are lost every year for describing the right feature in the wrong bars. Put a finger on the printed bar number, find it in the music as it plays, and only then write.

why.matters: Section A ends with eight marks on a piece you have never studied, and it is not the one question you cannot revise for. The specification promises that the extract is closely related to a set work, so it is built from materials you already know: a film cue in the style of *Star Wars*, a fusion, a Baroque aria. It comes with a skeleton score that shows one leading part and leaves out everything the question is about, which means everything printed is free and everything missing is worth marks. The vocabulary you learned for the set works is the vocabulary that scores here.

examples.title: The film cue you have never heard
examples.body: After studying *Star Wars* you might be handed a different cue in a similar style, not necessarily by the same composer or from the same film. What transfers is everything: a leitmotif on the brass, a late-Romantic orchestra, a march-like metre, a theme built from a wide leap. The same is true in every area of study. A Baroque aria over a repeating bass is Purcell's ground bass in another piece; a track with loops arriving and leaving is *Release* in another key. You are recognising materials, not guessing a title.

visual.alt: A table of four set works and the materials that transfer from each to an unfamiliar piece in the same style: leitmotif and brass, ground bass and word-painting, studio devices, loops and layers

examples.title: Everything printed is free
examples.body: A skeleton score gives you the key signature, the time signature, bar numbers and one leading part, sometimes with chord symbols and sometimes with gaps to fill. It does not give the other instruments, the texture, the dynamics or the articulation, and those are what the question asks for. So use the reading time to take the free information, the key, the metre, the first phrase, before a note is played, and spend the playings on what the page cannot tell you.

visual.alt: A table of what a skeleton score prints, key and time signatures, a leading part and bar numbers, against what it leaves out, the other instruments, the texture, the dynamics and the sound, which is where the marks are

examples.title: Pizzicato cello, not strings
examples.body: The mark schemes pay for the specific word. *Strings* is weak, *cello* is better, *pizzicato cello* is best; *percussion*, *drums*, *tabla*. So the sonority answer has two halves, the instrument and then the technique: plucked rather than bowed, two strings stopped at once, a tremolo, a harmonic, a slide, a muted trumpet, a melisma. Build that second vocabulary on purpose, because it is what separates a description of the sound from a name for it.

steps.title: One question, eight marks, a piece you have never heard
steps.body:
Section A ends with a question on a piece of music you have **never studied**. The specification fixes it at **8 marks** and prints a short **skeleton score** to go with it.

That sounds like the one question you cannot revise for. It is not, and here is why.

> The specification says the unfamiliar piece will be **"closely related to a set work (but not a set work)"**, and that its purpose is "for students to draw links from their study of the set works to the music heard as an unfamiliar extract".

The example the specification itself gives: after studying the Star Wars music, you might be handed a different film cue in a similar style — not necessarily the same composer, not necessarily the same film.

So the extract is deliberately built out of the same materials you already know. It comes from one of the four areas of study, it will sound like one of the eight set works, and every word you learned for that set work is a word you can use here.

One more boundary is worth knowing. The unfamiliar piece is **not** one of the suggested wider listening pieces in Appendix 4 either. Those are there to broaden your ear, not to be guessed at in the exam.

steps.title: Reading a skeleton score
steps.body:
Appendix 3 of the specification defines a skeleton score as:

> "A kind of notational summary — a visual aid for students in appraising examinations. It usually shows most or all of a **single leading part** rather than the complete texture."

Read that twice. The page is not the music. It is a map of the music, and it shows one line of it.

**What the score reliably gives you, before a note is played:**

- the **key signature**, so you know how many sharps or flats are in play
- the **time signature**, so you know how the beats are grouped
- **bar numbers**, printed every few bars, which every part of the question will refer to
- the **melody line** or another leading part, written out
- sometimes **chord symbols** printed above the stave
- sometimes deliberate **gaps**, where a part of the question asks you to fill something in

**What it does not give you:** the other instruments, the texture, the dynamics, the articulation, or anything at all about how it sounds. Those are the answers you are being asked for.

That asymmetry is the whole design of the question. Everything printed is free; everything missing is worth marks.

The cello is there; a skeleton score usually shows only one leading part
The cello must be an error in the recording and should be ignored

steps.title: Sonority: name the instrument, then name the technique
steps.body:
**Sonority** is defined in Appendix 3 as "the nature and quality of musical sounds". In practice the sonority parts of this question ask two things: *what* is playing, and *how* it is being played.

The mark schemes are consistently more generous to the specific word.

| Weak | Better | Best |
| --- | --- | --- |
| strings | cello | pizzicato cello |
| percussion | drums | tabla |
| brass | trumpet | muted trumpet |
| a keyboard | harpsichord | harpsichord continuo |

So build the second half of your vocabulary deliberately. These are the playing techniques Appendix 3 expects you to know by name:

- **Pizzicato** — a string plucked rather than bowed. Cancelled by *arco*.
- **Double stopping** — two or more strings stopped and played together.
- **Tremolo** — rapid repetition of one note, or of notes a third or more apart.
- **Harmonics** — a string touched lightly to sound a high, glassy pitch.
- **Glissando** — a slide through the notes between two pitches.
- **Portamento** — a slide smaller than a semitone; a voice can, a piano cannot.
- **Hammer on** and **pull off** — guitar techniques for fast playing without picking every note.
- **Wah wah** — a mute, on trumpet or trombone, that produces the sound it is named after. The same effect can be made in a studio.
- **Melisma** — many notes on one syllable. One note per syllable is **syllabic**.
- **Double tracking** and **overdubbing** — a part recorded twice, or added to a finished recording.

One more word that repays learning: **tessitura**, the part of a singer's range where the music mostly sits. A soprano line with a high tessitura sounds strained even when the actual top note is not extreme, and saying so is a grade 9 observation.

a slide through every note between two pitches

check.solution: **Pizzicato**. Appendix 3 defines it as playing where the strings are plucked rather than bowed, and notes that the direction is cancelled in a score by *arco*, meaning "with the bow".

steps.title: Texture: four words, used precisely
steps.body:
Texture is "the number of parts in a piece of music and how they relate to one another". Four words carry nearly all of the marks, and they are easy to mix up under pressure.

- **Monophony** — only one note sounds at a time: a single melodic line.
- **Homophony** — a melody with other, subsidiary, accompanying parts. The commonest texture in the repertoire.
- **Polyphony** — two or more simultaneous and largely independent melodies. Also called counterpoint.
- **Heterophony** — two or more parts playing the **same** melodic line at the same time, but with small variations between them.

The trap is monophony. Many students hear a large sound and rule it out. But a whole choir singing the same tune in unison is still **one melodic line**, and so still monophonic. Count the *lines*, not the people.

The second trap is heterophony against polyphony. Both have several parts moving at once. In polyphony the lines are **different** from one another; in heterophony they are the **same line**, decorated differently. Heterophony is common in the Fusions area of study and rare in the Western classical set works, which is itself a clue about where you are.

Some narrower words are worth having ready too:

- **Unison** — parts sounding exactly the same pitches.
- **Two-part**, **three-part**, **four-part** — literally how many lines there are.
- **Imitation** — one part states an idea and another follows with the same idea, the first carrying on underneath.
- **Call and response** — a phrase in one part answered by a phrase in another.
- **Continuo** — the Baroque bass line plus a chord-playing instrument realising the figured bass. Hearing one places the music before about 1750 straight away.
- **Accompaniment** — the background to a principal part.

each line is its own melody

steps.note: Forty voices, but every one of them is singing the same tune.

steps.text: One line means one note sounding at a time.
steps.note: That is the definition of monophony, whatever the volume.
Homophonic would need an accompaniment; polyphonic would need independent melodies.

check.solution: **Heterophony**: two or more parts playing the same melodic line simultaneously with small variations between them. Polyphony would need the lines to be different melodies; homophony would need one of them to be an accompaniment.

steps.title: Melodic and rhythmic devices worth naming
steps.body:
Several parts of the question will say **"name the melodic device"** or **"identify a harmonic device"**. They want a term, not a description. Here are the ones the specification defines.

**Melodic devices**

- **Sequence** — a melodic idea repeated at a different pitch. This is the single most commonly asked device in the whole paper.
- **Ostinato** — a short pattern repeated throughout a section. Called a **riff** in popular styles.
- **Imitation** — one part states an idea, another follows with it while the first continues.
- **Ornamentation** — decorating a melody: trills, turns, grace notes.
- **Monotone** — the same pitch used repeatedly.
- **Conjunct** (stepwise) and **disjunct** — moving by tones and semitones, or by leaps of a third or more.
- **Word painting** — the music illustrates the word: rising notes for "ascending".

**Rhythmic devices**

- **Syncopation** — a stressed note lands on a part of the bar or beat that would normally be weak.
- **Dotted rhythm** — a long dotted note paired with a short one.
- **Swung rhythm** — two equal written notes played long then short. A style built on them is **swing**.
- **Shuffle** — long and short alternating inside triplet groupings.
- **Triplet** — three notes in the time normally taken by two.

The difference between a **step** and a **leap** is defined, not a matter of opinion: a leap is any movement further than a tone or semitone, so a third or more.

rows: Up a second, do to re
Up a semitone, mi to fa
Up a third, do to mi
Up a fifth, do to so

props.centre: The device the paper asks for most often

boxes.title: Sequence
boxes.body: The same shape again at a different pitch. Look for a phrase that repeats a step higher or lower on the printed score.

boxes.title: Ostinato or riff
boxes.body: The same pattern at the same pitch, over and over. Riff is the word in popular and fusion styles.

boxes.title: Imitation
boxes.body: One part starts an idea, another takes it up while the first keeps going. Common in Baroque writing.

boxes.title: Pedal or drone
boxes.body: A note held or repeated while the chords above it change. This one is harmonic, not melodic.

check.prompt: A four-bar phrase is immediately repeated a tone lower, keeping the same shape. Name the device.
check.solution: A **sequence** is the repetition of a melody at a different pitch level. An ostinato would repeat at the *same* pitch; imitation would need a second part to take the idea up; syncopation is a rhythmic device, not a melodic one.

steps.title: Harmony you can read off the page
steps.body:
When chord symbols are printed above the melody, the harmony parts of the question stop being pure listening and become partly reading. Past papers have printed the chords for most of the extract and left a gap of one or two chords for you to complete, and have asked you to name a harmonic device in a given range of bars.

**Turning a chord symbol into a roman numeral.** Find the key from the key signature, then count up the scale to the chord's root.

In **G minor** the scale is G A B♭ C D E♭ F♯, so:

| Symbol | Degree | Roman numeral | Quality |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gm | 1 | i | minor |
| Cm | 4 | iv | minor |
| D or D7 | 5 | V or V7 | major |
| E♭ | 6 | VI | major |

Notice chord **V is major** even though the key is minor: the seventh degree is raised to F♯ to make it so. That raised note is the single clearest signal of a minor key in Western classical music.

**The four cadences**, exactly as the specification defines them:

- **Perfect** — V to I. It sounds finished.
- **Imperfect** — anything **to** V. It sounds unfinished, like a comma.
- **Plagal** — IV to I. The "Amen" cadence.
- **Interrupted** — V to VI. It sets up an ending and then refuses it.

**Harmonic devices** worth naming: a **pedal** (a held or repeated note, usually tonic or dominant, while chords change above it), a **drone** (the same idea in folk and fusion styles), a **ground bass** (a repeating bass phrase), **chromatic** chords, **dissonance**, **added** or **extended** chords such as added sevenths, **parallel motion**, and **modulation** to a new key.

props.title: The four cadences, named by the pair of chords

visuals.alt: A table pairing chords before and after a cadence with the name of the cadence they make

visuals.problem: The key signature has two flats and the melody ends on B flat. The last two chord symbols are F7 then B flat. Name the key and the cadence.

steps.text: Two flats and an ending on B flat means B flat major.
steps.note: B flat major and G minor share the signature; the final note decides it.

steps.text: B flat is the tonic, so B flat is chord I.
steps.note: Built on the scale it is a major triad.

steps.text: F is five notes up from B flat, so F7 is chord V7.
steps.note: F A C E flat is a dominant seventh.

steps.text: V7 to I is a perfect cadence.
steps.note: It is the cadence that sounds finished, which is why pieces end with it.

check.prompt: A phrase in C major ends on the chord G, having come from the chord F. Name the cadence.
check.solution: In C major, G is chord V. Any chord moving **to** V makes an **imperfect** cadence, and it sounds unfinished. A perfect cadence would need V moving to I; plagal is IV to I; interrupted is V to VI.

markScheme.description: imperfect

steps.title: A whole unfamiliar question, worked
steps.body:
Here is an extract in the style of the Instrumental Music area of study, with everything the paper would give you. Work through it as five separate small questions, one per playing.

**What is printed on the paper**

- Key signature: two flats. The melody begins and ends on G.
- Time signature: three crotchets in a bar.
- Bar numbers printed at bars 1, 5, 9, 13, 17 and 21.
- The violin line notated throughout, with chord symbols above it.
- Chord symbols: bars 1 to 4 **Gm | Gm | Cm | D7**, bars 5 to 8 **Gm | E♭ | Cm | D7**, bars 9 to 12 **Gm | Gm | Gm | Gm**.

**What you hear**

- Bars 1 to 4: the violin alone.
- Bars 5 to 8: a harpsichord and a cello join, the harpsichord filling in the chords.
- Bars 5 to 8 in the violin: the bars 1 to 4 phrase again, starting a tone lower.
- Bars 9 to 12: the cello holds a single low G while the violin runs above it.
- Bars 13 to 20: the violin and a second violin chase the same idea, the second entering a bar later while the first carries on.
- Bars 21 to 24: all parts together, ending on a long G.

The working below takes it part by part.

visuals.problem: (a) Name the key. (b) Identify the texture in bars 1 to 4. (c) Name the melodic device in bars 5 to 8. (d) Name the cadence at bar 4 into bar 5. (e) Identify a harmonic device in bars 9 to 12.

steps.text: (a) Two flats, and the melody begins and ends on G: G minor.
steps.note: Two flats is B flat major or G minor. The note the music settles on decides between them.

steps.text: The chord symbol D7 confirms it.
steps.note: D7 has an F sharp, the raised seventh of G minor, giving a major chord V in a minor key.

steps.text: (b) Bars 1 to 4 are the violin alone, so one line: monophony.
steps.note: A single melodic line with nothing sounding against it. The number of instruments is one, but it would still be monophonic if ten violins played it in unison.

steps.text: (c) Bars 5 to 8 repeat bars 1 to 4 a tone lower: a sequence.
steps.note: The same shape at a different pitch. Not an ostinato, which would repeat at the same pitch.

steps.text: (d) Bar 4 is D7 and bar 5 is Gm, that is V7 to i: a perfect cadence.
steps.note: It sounds finished, which is why the phrase feels closed before the sequence starts again.

steps.text: (e) Bars 9 to 12 hold a low G under changing violin writing: a tonic pedal.
steps.note: A pedal is a sustained or repeated note, usually tonic or dominant, held while the music above it moves.

rows: the opening phrase a tone lower
harpsichord and cello filling in the harmony
a held low G under moving parts
the second violin takes up the idea a bar later

check.prompt: In that worked extract, a harpsichord fills in the chords above a cello bass line from bar 5. What is the Baroque name for this pairing?
check.solution: It is the **continuo** (or basso continuo): a bass line played by a low string instrument together with a chord-playing instrument such as a harpsichord, organ or lute, which completes the harmony by realising the figured bass. Hearing one places the music firmly in the Baroque period.

steps.title: Answer the command word, in the words asked for
steps.body:
Appendix 5 of the specification defines every command word the paper uses. Learning them is worth marks, because each one tells you the shape of the answer.

| Command word | What it wants |
| --- | --- |
| State, give, name, identify, list | one or more points; recall or find factual information |
| Complete | fill in blanks, for example on a score |
| Describe | points, which may or may not be linked; if linked, in the correct order |
| Explain | points joined to a justification or extension |
| Compare | similarities and differences, with relative judgements |
| Analyse | examine and dissect musical elements in detail, and how they combine to create an effect |
| Evaluate | judgements against parameters, and conclusions |

In the unfamiliar question the commands are almost always at the top of that table — *identify*, *name*, *complete*. That matters more than it looks.

> "Identify the texture in bars 1 to 4" is a one-mark, one-word question. The correct answer is *homophonic*. Writing three sentences about the texture earns exactly the same one mark, and costs you time you need for the twelve-mark essay.

Two more habits separate a grade 9 answer here.

**Give the number of answers asked for, and no more.** Mark schemes say "any two of the following". If you write three and one is wrong, examiners take them in order, so your wrong third is not a free extra — it can replace a right one.

**Name the feature before the effect.** In the extended-answer mark schemes, every appraising point is credited only where a musical observation supports it. That habit is worth building here even in one-word answers: *dotted rhythms*, not *it sounds military*.

Identify a harmonic device in bars 23 to 27. (1)
Identify how instrumentation establishes the mood. (2)
Two separate points, each naming an instrument or technique

steps.title: What to carry into the exam
steps.body:
- The unfamiliar question is worth **8 marks** and comes with a **skeleton score**.
- The piece is **closely related to a set work but is never one**, and never one of the suggested wider listening pieces either. Work out which set work it stands beside and use that vocabulary.
- A skeleton score is a **summary of one leading part**. Instruments that are not printed are still playing.
- Read the key signature, time signature, bar numbers and any chord symbols in the reading time.
- **Sonority**: name the instrument, then the technique. *Pizzicato cello*, not *strings*.
- **Texture**: count the lines, not the people. Monophony is one line; homophony is melody plus accompaniment; polyphony is independent melodies; heterophony is the same melody decorated differently.
- **Melodic devices**: sequence, ostinato or riff, imitation, ornamentation, monotone, conjunct and disjunct.
- **Rhythmic devices**: syncopation, dotted, swung, shuffle, triplet.
- **Harmony**: read the chord symbols, name the roman numerals, and know the four cadences — perfect V to I, imperfect to V, plagal IV to I, interrupted V to VI.
- Answer the **command word** in the number of words it asks for, and leave nothing blank.

questions.prompt: Two violins play two different melodies at the same time, neither accompanying the other. Name the texture.
questions.solution: Two or more simultaneous and largely independent melody lines is **polyphony**, also called counterpoint. Homophony would need one line to be an accompaniment; heterophony would need them to be the same line, decorated differently.

markScheme.description: polyphonic

questions.prompt: In an extract, the tabla plays the same two-bar rhythmic pattern over and over for eight bars without changing. Name the device.
questions.solution: An **ostinato** is a short musical pattern repeated throughout a section or a whole piece. In popular styles the same idea is called a **riff**. A sequence would repeat at a *different* pitch; imitation needs a second part to take the idea up; modulation is a change of key.

markScheme.description: ostinato (accept riff)

questions.prompt: A cello holds one low note for eight bars while the chords above it keep changing. Give the term for this.
questions.solution: A **pedal** (or pedal point): a note, usually the tonic or the dominant, sustained or repeated while the chords change above it, often creating dissonance on the way. In folk and fusion styles the same idea is usually called a **drone**.

markScheme.description: pedal

questions.prompt: A skeleton score has two flats in the key signature and the melody begins and ends on G. Above bar 8 the chord symbol D7 is printed. Which chord of the key is that?
questions.solution: Two flats with the music settling on G is **G minor**. D is the fifth degree of that scale, so D7 is **V7**. Its F sharp is the raised seventh of the minor scale, which is what makes chord V major in a minor key.

markScheme.description: chord V7

questions.prompt: In an extract in four-four time, the stressed notes keep landing on the second half of beats 2 and 4 rather than on the beats themselves. Name the rhythmic device.
questions.solution: **Syncopation**: a strong or stressed note occurring on a part of the bar or beat that would normally be weak or unstressed. A triplet is three notes in the time of two; a dotted rhythm is a long note paired with a short one; a glissando is a slide and is not a rhythmic device at all.

markScheme.description: syncopation

questions.prompt: A flute and a voice perform the same melody at the same time, the voice ornamenting it with slides while the flute plays it plainly. Give the one-word term for this texture.
questions.solution: **Heterophonic**. Heterophony is where two or more parts play the same melodic line simultaneously but with small variations between them. It is common in the Fusions area of study and rare in the Western classical set works, so hearing it is itself a clue about where the extract comes from.

markScheme.description: heterophonic

questions.prompt: Put these jobs in the order you should do them in an unfamiliar listening question.
items: Read the score for key, metre, bar numbers and chord symbols
Name the instruments and the playing techniques you can hear
Decide the texture of the bars each part of the question names
Name the melodic and rhythmic devices the question asks for
Fill in any chord gaps and check that nothing has been left blank
questions.solution: Reading comes first because it is free: the key, the metre, the bar numbers and any chord symbols are on the page before a note is played. Sonority comes next, because what is playing is the easiest thing to catch on a first hearing and it frames everything else. Texture follows, then the devices, which need you to have heard a phrase more than once. Chords and the final check come last, because the chord symbols are partly printed and so need the least listening.

markScheme.description: reading the printed score before any listening
sonority before texture and devices
chords and the final check last

questions.prompt: An extract has two flats in the key signature and settles on G. Bar 15 carries the chord symbol Cm and bar 16 carries Gm. Name the cadence.
questions.solution: The key is G minor, so Cm is chord iv and Gm is chord i. Chord IV moving to chord I is a **plagal** cadence — the "Amen" cadence. A perfect cadence would need V to I, which here would be D or D7 moving to Gm.

markScheme.description: plagal

questions.prompt: Which of these is a harmonic device rather than a melodic one?
questions.solution: A **pedal** is harmonic: it is a held or repeated note underneath *changing chords*, and its interest is in the harmony it creates against them. A sequence, imitation and ornamentation are all things done to a melodic line, which is why the specification calls them melodic devices.

markScheme.description: a tonic pedal

questions.prompt: A skeleton score is in three-four time. The passage a question asks about runs from bar 9 to bar 24 inclusive. How many crotchet beats does that passage last?
questions.solution: Bar 9 to bar 24 inclusive is 16 bars, because both end bars count. Three-four holds 3 crotchets in a bar, so the passage lasts 16 times 3, which is 48 crotchet beats. Counting 24 minus 9 gives 15 and is the usual slip.

markScheme.description: 16 bars inclusive times 3 crotchets = 48

questions.prompt:
An extract in the Fusions area of study is played several times, with a skeleton score showing the flute line only.

**On the page:** four sharps in the key signature; four crotchets in a bar; bar numbers at 1, 9, 17 and 25.

**What you hear:**

- A synthesiser holds a low D right through the extract, never changing.
- Bars 1 to 8: tabla and dhol alone, playing a two-bar pattern four times over, with the accents falling on the second half of beat 2 and the second half of beat 4.
- Bars 9 to 16: a bamboo flute enters with a four-bar melody that uses only the notes D, E, F sharp, A and B.
- Bars 17 to 24: a voice sings the same melody as the flute at the same time, ornamenting it with slides and turns while the flute plays it plainly.
- Bars 25 to 32: the flute plays a two-bar phrase, the voice answers with a two-bar phrase, and this alternates.

Analyse how this extract combines two musical traditions, referring to sonority, texture, tonality and rhythm.
questions.solution:
The extract is a fusion in the literal sense: two sets of instruments, two habits of melody, laid over one frame.

**Sonority.** The percussion is South Asian — tabla and dhol — and the melody instrument is a bamboo flute, joined later by a solo voice. Against these sits a synthesiser, which belongs to Western studio practice. Nothing about the recording tries to disguise the join; the two groups keep their own timbres.

**Texture.** The synthesiser's low D sounds throughout and never changes, so it is a **drone** rather than a chord part. Bars 1 to 8 are drone and percussion only, so there is no melody at all yet. From bar 9 the flute supplies one melodic line over the drone. Bars 17 to 24 are the most interesting texture in the extract: the voice sings the flute's melody at the same time but ornaments it with slides and turns while the flute plays it plainly. That is **heterophony** — the same line, small variations — and it is characteristic of the Fusions area of study rather than of Western classical music, where two singers over a drone would more often be in harmony. Bars 25 to 32 change again to **call and response**, two bars of flute answered by two bars of voice.

**Tonality.** The flute uses only D, E, F sharp, A and B: five notes, and exactly degrees 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 of D major, which makes it the **D major pentatonic**. Pentatonic writing has no semitone steps, so the melody never pulls towards a leading note and never needs a cadence. With the drone underneath and no changing chords, the harmony does not move at all — there is tonality without functional harmony, which is what lets the two traditions sit together without one having to give way.

**Rhythm.** The tabla and dhol play a two-bar pattern four times over in bars 1 to 8: a repeated pattern at the same pitch is an **ostinato**. Its accents fall on the second half of beat 2 and the second half of beat 4, that is, on parts of the bar that would normally be weak, so the pattern is **syncopated**. Against a drone that never moves, that syncopation is the only thing generating momentum, and it carries the whole opening.

**Overall.** Sonority and rhythm come from one tradition and the sustained electronic drone from another, while the pentatonic melody and heterophonic decoration belong comfortably to both. The fusion works because neither tradition is asked to do something it does not do: there is no Western harmonic progression to fight the drone, and no notated ornamentation to flatten the vocal line.

questions.prompt:
An extract in the Music for Stage and Screen area of study is played several times, with a skeleton score showing the top line and chord symbols above it.

**On the page:** two flats in the key signature; four crotchets in a bar; the melody begins and ends on B flat. The chord symbols printed for bars 5 to 12 are B♭ | Gm | E♭ | F7 | B♭ | Gm | E♭ | F7, and bar 13 is B♭.

**What you hear:**

- Bars 1 to 4: trumpets and horns in octaves, very loud, using only the notes B flat, D and F, in dotted rhythms, with a triplet on the last beat of bar 2.
- Bars 5 to 12: violins take a broad melody, brass hold long notes underneath, and a timpani roll runs under the whole passage.
- Bars 13 to 20: the bars 5 to 8 melody returns a third higher, played by the full orchestra.
- Bar 20: a cymbal crash and a final long chord.

Analyse how the composer uses instrumentation, rhythm and harmony to establish a heroic mood, referring to the bar numbers given.
questions.solution:
**Instrumentation.** The extract opens with trumpets and horns in octaves at a very loud dynamic. Brass in octaves is the loudest, most penetrating sound an orchestra has and carries no harmony of its own, so the opening reads as a summons rather than as a tune. The notes used are only B flat, D and F — the notes of the tonic triad — which makes the opening a **fanfare**, and fanfares carry a ceremonial association the listener recognises immediately. From bar 5 the violins take a broad melody while the brass hold long notes underneath and a timpani roll runs through, so the brass move from stating to supporting. Bars 13 to 20 bring the full orchestra, and the cymbal crash at bar 20 marks the end.

**Rhythm.** Bars 1 to 4 are in dotted rhythms: a long dotted note paired with a short one, repeatedly. Dotted rhythms are the rhythm of a march and of a military fanfare, and they give a sharpness that even notes would not. The triplet on the last beat of bar 2 — three notes in the time of two — pushes the phrase forward across the barline instead of letting it settle. Both devices are doing the same job: keeping the opening urgent.

**Harmony.** Two flats in the key signature with the melody beginning and ending on B flat gives **B flat major**. The printed chord symbols then read straight off as roman numerals: B flat is **I**, G minor is **vi**, E flat is **IV** and F7 is **V7**. That is an entirely **functional** progression, with no chromatic chords at all, which is what makes the passage sound confident rather than uneasy. Bar 12 is F7 and bar 13 is B flat, so V7 moving to I gives a **perfect cadence** — the cadence that sounds finished — arriving exactly where the full orchestra enters.

**Structure and device.** The four chords fill bars 5 to 8 and are then repeated for bars 9 to 12, so the whole passage sits on a **repeated chord pattern**. That repetition is what allows the ear to expect the cadence at bar 13 before it arrives. At bar 13 the bars 5 to 8 melody returns a third higher: the same shape at a different pitch is a **sequence**, and raising it lifts the tessitura of every part, which is heard as an increase in effort and brightness. Combined with the full orchestral entry, that is the climax of the extract.

**Overall.** Nothing here is subtle, and that is the point. A fanfare on the tonic triad, dotted rhythms, entirely functional harmony, a perfect cadence timed to the loudest entry, and a rising sequence at the climax: each element is a familiar signal, and they all point the same way.

questions.prompt: Appendix 5 of the specification defines the command words. What does "analyse" ask you to do?
options: Recall factual information and name it
Examine and dissect musical elements in detail
Fill in the blanks on a printed score
questions.solution: **Analyse** means "examine, dissect musical elements in detail" and "focus on individual musical elements and how they combine to create an effect or achieve a purpose". Recalling and naming is *state, give, name, identify, list*; judging and concluding is *evaluate*; filling in blanks is *complete*.

markScheme.description: examine and dissect musical elements in detail

questions.prompt: A part of the unfamiliar question is worth 2 marks and the mark scheme reads "any two of the following". What should you write?
options: Exactly two answers, each naming one feature
Four answers, so two of them must be right
One answer, developed into a paragraph
Two answers plus a sentence of explanation
questions.solution: Two marks, two answers, each naming a musical feature. Writing four does not improve your chances: examiners mark the answers in the order given, so a wrong one can take the place of a right one. Extra explanation is not wrong but earns nothing here and costs time needed for the twelve-mark question.

questions.prompt:
An extract in the Vocal Music area of study is played several times, with a skeleton score showing the vocal line and chord symbols above it.

**On the page:** no sharps or flats; four crotchets in a bar; the chord symbols printed for bars 13 to 20 are C | Am | F | G7 | C | Am | F | G7, and bar 21 is C.

**What you hear:**

- Bars 1 to 12: one voice with an acoustic guitar strumming chords behind it, one note to each syllable, and the melody stays inside a fifth.
- Bars 13 to 20: bass guitar and drum kit enter; three vocal parts sing in harmony; the top part stretches the title word over eleven notes.
- The lead voice in bars 13 to 20 has clearly been recorded twice and the two takes laid over each other.
- Bars 21 to 28: an electric guitar plays the bars 13 to 16 tune a fifth higher, bending some notes and using hammer ons.
- Bars 29 to 36: the bars 13 to 20 music again, with the drums dropping out for the last four bars.

Analyse how this extract is put together, referring to structure, texture, melody, sonority and harmony.
questions.solution:
**Structure.** The extract falls into clear blocks: bars 1 to 12 are a **verse**, bars 13 to 20 a **chorus**, bars 21 to 28 an **instrumental** or guitar solo, and bars 29 to 36 the chorus again. Verse and chorus form is the standard structure of popular song, and every change of block here is marked by a change of forces as well as of material, so the shape is audible without counting bars.

**Texture.** The verse is **homophonic** and thin: one voice with an acoustic guitar strumming chords behind it, so there is a single melodic line and an accompaniment. The chorus thickens in two ways at once — bass guitar and drum kit enter, and the single voice becomes three parts in harmony. That is still homophony, since the lower two voices support the top line rather than pursuing melodies of their own, but the increase in density is what makes the chorus sound like an arrival. In the last four bars the drums drop out, thinning the texture again, which is a common way of signalling an ending without slowing down.

**Melody.** The verse is **syllabic** — one note to each syllable — and stays within a fifth, so it is narrow and conversational, and it leaves the singer somewhere to go. The chorus does the opposite: the top part stretches the title word over eleven notes, which is a **melisma**, and the wide contrast between the two makes the hook stand out. The guitar solo takes the bars 13 to 16 tune a fifth higher, so it is a **sequence**, and putting it in the guitar's brighter register is what gives the solo its lift.

**Sonority.** The accompaniment moves from acoustic guitar to a full band, and the lead voice in the chorus has been recorded twice with the takes laid over each other — **double tracking**, a studio effect that thickens and slightly blurs a voice, and one that cannot be produced live. The guitar solo uses **string bends** and **hammer ons**, the second being a technique for playing fast without picking every note.

**Harmony.** No sharps or flats, and the music settles on C, so the key is **C major**. The printed chorus chords read as **I, vi, IV, V7** — C, A minor, F, G7 — repeated for bars 17 to 20, so the chorus sits on a **repeated chord sequence**. Bar 20 is G7 and bar 21 is C, so V7 to I gives a **perfect cadence** exactly where the guitar solo begins, which is why the solo feels like a fresh start rather than a continuation.

**Overall.** Every element changes at the same moments. Forces, texture, melodic style and register all shift at bar 13 and again at bar 21, and the harmony underneath stays entirely functional throughout, so the listener has a stable frame against which those changes register.

examTechnique.body:
**Know the shape before you sit down.** One question in Section A is on an unfamiliar piece, and the specification fixes it at **8 marks**. A short **skeleton score** is printed. The extract is played several times; the paper prints how many and the audio announces it.

**Work out which set work it is standing next to.** The specification says the unfamiliar piece is "closely related to a set work (but not a set work)" — the example it gives is that after studying the Star Wars music you might be given a different film cue in a similar style. Naming that relationship in your head tells you which vocabulary to reach for.

**Read the score in the reading time.** Key signature, time signature, bar numbers, and any chord symbols printed above the melody. All of it is free.

**Use one playing per question part, not one playing for everything.** There are usually five or six short parts. Decide before the first playing which part you will settle on each hearing.

**Answer the command word.** *Identify* and *name* want a word. *Describe* wants points. *Explain* wants a point joined to a reason. Appendix 5 of the specification defines them all, and the paper uses them precisely.

**Where the paper says "any two", give two.** A third answer earns nothing and the first wrong one can cost you.

**Say what is playing, not just that something is.** "Strings" is weaker than "pizzicato cello"; "percussion" is weaker than "tabla". The mark schemes reward the specific word.

**Do not leave a part blank.** A one-word answer costs seconds. A blank is the only guaranteed zero on the page.
examinerErrors: Treating the skeleton score as the full texture, then failing to mention instruments that are clearly playing but are not notated.
Answering about the wrong bars, because the bar numbers on the page were never matched to the music as it played.
Writing a paragraph where the paper asked for one word, and running out of time in Section B.
Naming a general family — "brass", "percussion" — where the mark scheme wanted a specific instrument.
Giving three answers where two were asked for, so the wrong one is the one that gets marked.
Describing an effect without naming the musical feature that causes it.
Ignoring the chord symbols printed above the melody, then guessing at the harmony questions.
Forgetting that the piece is deliberately close to a set work, and so not using the vocabulary already learned for it.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer has read the skeleton score before a note is played and has already noticed the key, the metre and the printed chord symbols. It recognises within a few bars which area of study the extract belongs to and which set work it sits beside, and it reaches for that vocabulary deliberately. It names instruments and techniques precisely — pizzicato cello rather than strings, tabla rather than drums — and it uses the four texture words correctly, including knowing that a choir singing in unison is still monophonic. It answers each part in the number of words asked for, matches every answer to the bar numbers in the question, and leaves nothing blank.
